strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated use of reinforcement learning for 3D scene editing, turning the hard generation problem into a tractable verification problem with a 3D foundation model as reward.
Uses VGGT confidence maps and relative pose errors as geometry-aware rewards, with an anchor reward to preserve 2D editing fidelity; the empirical confidence-consistency correlation is convincing.
Single-pass RL-finetuned editor avoids per-scene optimization and is much faster at inference, while ablations show transfer to another 2D backbone (Qwen-Image-Edit).

Quantitative and qualitative comparisons indicate substantial improvements in editing fidelity, semantic alignment, and multi-view consistency over strong baselines, with ablations validating reward components and exposing reward hacking in SfM/reprojection verifiers.
Paper is generally clear, includes limitations and future work, and promises code/model release.
weaknesses: Training and evaluation scale is very limited: only 8 scenes, 70 prompts, 1,319 samples, and the main 70 in-distribution novel-view cases appear to use the same scenes/instructions as training; only 30/100 test cases are unseen, which weakens broad generalization and SoTA claims.

The anchor reward only directly supervises one randomly chosen anchor view via LPIPS, while VGGT consistency for the other views substitutes the offline anchor for the model's generated anchor; this may not directly enforce that the model's own anchor view is consistent with its generated non-anchor views, potentially limiting true multi-view coherence.

The main VIEScore metric relies on GPT-4.1 and is presented as objective/reproducible, but VLM-based evaluation can be noisy and sensitive to prompt/style bias; CLIP and Ph-Loss improvements are smaller, and the paper itself shows Ph-Loss can be reward-hacked, making the consistency evidence less conclusive.

Key implementation details—3DGS reconstruction from edited views, whether editing time includes reconstruction, data splits, pre-edit filtering, reward weights, and GRPO details—are deferred to the appendix, limiting assessment of reproducibility from the main paper.

No comparison is provided against concurrent/stronger FLUX-Kontext-based or recent multi-view consistent editing methods such as Tinker, and the re-implemented baseline may not be optimized to the same extent as the proposed RL training.

The VGGT reward may penalize valid geometry-changing edits if the edited content is out of its training distribution, and the paper does not fully analyze failure cases where confidence drops for reasons other than multi-view inconsistency.
Training is computationally heavy (42 hours for one epoch on limited data) with a small dataset, so the claimed efficiency and scalability trade-offs are not fully explored.

strengths: The paper introduces a timely and conceptually interesting direction: using reinforcement learning, specifically GRPO-style optimization, to improve multi-view consistency in 3D scene editing without paired 3D-consistent supervision.

The central observation that generating 3D-consistent edited views is hard while verifying consistency is more tractable is clearly motivated, and the use of VGGT as a frozen geometry-aware reward model is a plausible and original idea.

The proposed reward design combines VGGT confidence, relative camera pose, and an anchor-view fidelity reward, and the qualitative examples and ablations provide some evidence that these components matter.
The method aims for single-pass inference after RL fine-tuning, avoiding per-scene optimization, and the reported editing time is attractive if the claims hold up.
The paper shows that the fine-tuned editor can preserve much of the original 2D editing ability and can be transferred to another backbone such as Qwen-Image-Edit, which is a useful direction.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is unclear and potentially biased. The model is trained on only 8 scenes and 70 prompts, while the main comparison includes 70 "novel view" cases that may share the same scenes and instructions as training. The zero-shot cases are mostly qualitative or relegated to an unavailable appendix, so the claimed generalization is not adequately supported in the main paper.

The comparison to prior work is not convincing. Most baselines use InstructPix2Pix, a much weaker 2D editor, so the large gains may be largely attributable to FLUX-Kontext rather than the proposed RL framework. The closest baseline, Tinker, also uses FLUX-Kontext and is discussed as a key prior method but is not empirically compared.

The VGGT-based reward is vulnerable to reward hacking and is not sufficiently validated. A correlation between VGGT confidence and consistency degradation does not prove that optimizing VGGT confidence yields semantically correct and sharp multi-view edits. The anchor reward supervises only one view, leaving other views without direct editing-fidelity supervision; the paper does not rule out blurry, low-frequency, or out-of-distribution solutions that VGGT scores highly.

The metrics are not fully reliable. VIEScore with GPT-4.1 is not obviously objective or reproducible, Ph-Loss is shown in the paper itself to be gameable, and no error bars or statistical significance tests are reported. A proper user study or more robust 3D consistency metric is needed to substantiate the main claims.

The experimental scale is very limited: 1,319 training samples, 8 training scenes, 42 hours of training, and ablations on roughly 200 face samples. This is weak support for claims of state-of-the-art quality and broad generalization. The paper also does not report per-split quantitative results in the main text, making it difficult to assess in-distribution versus zero-shot performance.

Citation and attribution errors are serious. For example, VGGT is cited as [48], but reference [48] is an unrelated space-physics paper; GRPO is cited with duplicated/incorrect references [17,18]; Qwen-Image-Edit is cited as [57] but that reference points to a different paper; and [15] duplicates [14]. These errors undermine reproducibility and scholarly rigor.

The efficiency claim is potentially misleading. It is unclear whether the reported 1.5-minute editing time includes the final 3DGS reconstruction from edited images, which is part of the pipeline. If reconstruction is excluded, the speed comparison against per-scene optimization methods is not apples-to-apples.

The relative pose reward enforces alignment with ground-truth relative poses, but the method claims to handle geometry-changing edits. The interaction between this reward and legitimate edits that alter geometry is not analyzed, and could bias the model toward preserving the original camera/content arrangement inappropriately.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel and well-motivated RL framework for 3D scene editing, correctly identifying the asymmetry that generating multi-view consistent images is hard while verifying consistency is tractable; this is a compelling basis for RL.

The reward design is creative and technically sound: using VGGT's confidence maps and relative pose predictions as a 3D consistency verifier is well justified, and the empirical analysis (near-linear correlation between consistency degradation and confidence drop) supports this choice.

Extensive experiments show strong quantitative and qualitative improvements over open-source SoTA methods, with large gains in VIEScore (5.48 vs 3.23), better CLIP-dir, lowest photometric reprojection loss, and over 2x faster editing than optimization-based baselines.

The ablation study is thorough, validating each reward component, showing VGGT's advantage over SfM and reprojection-based rewards (which suffer from reward hacking), and demonstrating transferability to a stronger 2D backbone (Qwen-Image-Edit).

The anchor reward is a sensible mechanism to preserve the powerful 2D editor's fidelity while learning 3D consistency, and the method generalizes to unseen instructions and scenes without per-scene fine-tuning at inference.
weaknesses: The reference list contains serious errors and duplicates: VGGT is cited as [48] but the entry points to an unrelated paper on proton isotropy boundaries; multiple references are duplicated (e.g., InstructPix2Pix [3]/[4], DreamFusion [37]/[38], DeepSeek-R1 [17]/[18], Godard et al. [14]/[15]) and the citation for streaming/causal attention [15] attributes it to a self-supervised depth estimation paper. These errors harm reproducibility and credibility.

Training scale is very limited: only 8 scenes (1,319 samples) with 42 hours of GRPO training on a single A6000. The zero-shot evaluation uses only 14 new scenes, which may not sufficiently support strong generalization claims.

The paper lacks a comparison with Tinker, a highly relevant concurrent method that also uses FLUX-Kontext and targets multi-view consistent 3D editing. If Tinker is unavailable or not open-source, the authors should explicitly justify its omission.

The reward design may still be vulnerable to implicit reward hacking: while VGGT is shown to be more robust than SfM and photometric warping, no adversarial analysis is provided to probe whether the model could generate images that VGGT is confident about yet are semantically incorrect or over-smoothed.

In a given GRPO group, the anchor view's own multi-view consistency is not directly rewarded; it is only optimized via LPIPS against a pre-edited single-view result, while other views are checked against that anchor. The paper does not analyze whether this asymmetry could propagate inconsistencies in the final 3DGS reconstruction.

Some claims are overstated: 'optimization-free' at inference still requires per-scene 3DGS reconstruction, and the '2x faster' claim compares to the original EditSplat rather than the stronger FLUX-Kontext baseline (which is 20x slower). Key details (formal GRPO objective, Ph-Loss, SfM reward, user study) are relegated to the appendix and not fully defined in the main paper.

Evaluation relies on VLM-based VIEScore and 2D CLIP directional similarity, which may not fully capture 3D consistency and editing fidelity; no human study is included in the main paper, and the main quantitative table mixes in-distribution and zero-shot cases without per-split breakdown (which appears only in the appendix).

strengths: The paper presents a novel and well-motivated framework, RL3DEdit, that uses reinforcement learning to inject 3D multi-view consistency into a strong 2D editor while avoiding scarce paired 3D editing data.

The core insight that generating 3D-consistent edits is hard but verifying 3D consistency is tractable is convincingly developed and supported by the empirical analysis showing that VGGT confidence maps correlate with multi-view consistency.

The method is technically sound in its main components: multi-image joint editing with FLUX-Kontext, GRPO-based fine-tuning, and a composite reward combining VGGT depth/point confidence, relative pose alignment, and an anchor LPIPS reward.

The reward design is well ablated. The paper shows that naive SfM and photometric reprojection rewards are vulnerable to reward hacking, while the VGGT-based reward better preserves image quality and consistency.

The experimental evidence is broad: comparisons with DGE, GaussCtrl, EditSplat, and a reimplemented EditSplat with FLUX-Kontext; quantitative metrics, qualitative comparisons, user study, zero-shot tests, and an extension to Qwen-Image-Edit.

The method achieves strong practical efficiency, reporting 1.5 minutes average editing time versus 3.5 minutes to 40 minutes for baselines, and demonstrates clear qualitative improvements on challenging editing types such as motion, replacement, style transfer, and scene addition.

The paper is generally clear, includes detailed implementation and dataset information in the supplementary material, discusses limitations, and promises code/model release, which supports reproducibility.

The work is original in bringing RL with a 3D foundation-model verifier into the 3D scene editing pipeline, and it has promising potential impact for future 3D editing and RL-based 3D consistency research.
weaknesses: The training scale is very limited: only 8 scenes, 70 prompts, and 1,319 samples. Although the paper demonstrates some zero-shot generalization to 4 new scenes and 16 unseen instructions, the evidence for broad generalization and scalability remains modest.

VGGT confidence as a reward may bias optimization toward photorealistic or VGGT-familiar geometry. Stylized, artistic, and strongly geometry-changing edits may be penalized by the reward, and the anchor reward only partially mitigates this risk.

The comparison protocol is not fully conclusive. The paper does not compare with the recent Tinker method despite discussing it as a powerful FLUX-based baseline, and most baselines use the weaker InstructPix2Pix backbone while only one reimplemented baseline uses FLUX-Kontext.

The evaluation relies heavily on VIEScore with GPT-4.1, which can be noisy and difficult to reproduce exactly. The large VIEScore gap is not fully mirrored by CLIP directional similarity or photometric reprojection loss, where improvements are relatively modest.

The claim of being optimization-free or single-pass is somewhat overstated. Although there is no per-scene or per-prompt editing-model fine-tuning, inference still requires multi-step diffusion sampling and per-scene 3DGS reconstruction optimization, including AnySplat warm-up and 3,000 iterations.

The ablation studies are conducted only on face scenes, which may not fully validate the reward-weight and design choices across the diverse scene types and editing instructions used in the main experiments.

Some technical details and notation need clarification. For example, the VGGT geometry loss in the main text appears to contain a repeated variable rather than a target variable, and reward normalization, anchor filtering, and exact inference settings could be described more precisely.
Broader societal impacts, potential misuse of 3D scene editing, and dataset licensing details are not discussed in depth, although these are not central to the scientific contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and timely problem: 3D-consistent scene editing without paired 3D editing data. The idea of using RL with a 3D foundation model as a verifiable reward is novel and interesting.

The reward design is reasonably motivated: VGGT confidence maps, relative pose errors, and an anchor-based perceptual reward jointly aim to enforce multi-view consistency while preserving 2D editing fidelity. The empirical analysis in Fig. 5 showing confidence degradation under increasing inconsistency is a useful observation.

The results, if taken at face value, are strong: RL3DEdit reports large gains over prior methods on VIEScore, CLIP directional similarity, and photometric reprojection loss, while reducing editing time. The qualitative figures cover diverse edits, including motion, replacement, style, background, and addition.

The paper includes ablations on reward components, alternative verifiers, anchor selection, denoising steps, and reward weights. It also discusses limitations and extensions to another 2D editor (Qwen-Image-Edit), which strengthens the empirical study.
weaknesses: The reference list contains many suspicious, unrelated, or future-dated citations (e.g., [2], [4], [15], [20], [38], [51], [52], [75]) that are cited in contexts unrelated to 3D editing, such as broad claims about deep learning. This is a serious scholarly concern and suggests careless or possibly fabricated references, undermining confidence in the manuscript.

The claimed 'single-pass' and 'optimization-free' inference is overstated: the method still requires 3DGS reconstruction and optimization (~40s) and relies on GT camera poses. It is not a fully feed-forward, optimization-free pipeline in the usual sense.

The evaluation is limited. Training uses only 8 scenes and 70 prompts; the test set has 100 cases, with only 14 new scenes and 16 unseen instructions. Claims of zero-shot generalization from such a small training set need much stronger validation.

Important baselines are missing or weakly compared. There is no direct comparison to unedited multi-view FLUX-Kontext editing with 3DGS reconstruction, nor to Tinker, a recent FLUX-Kontext-based 3D editing method. Baselines using InstructPix2Pix are clearly disadvantaged, and even the reimplemented EditSplat-with-FLUX baseline may not have been optimally tuned.

The core VGGT reward is not fully validated as a robustness guarantee. Confidence maps may correlate with textureness, blur, or inherent prediction difficulty rather than pure multi-view consistency, leaving room for reward hacking. The ablations on alternative verifiers are conducted only on face scenes with ~200 samples, not on the full diverse dataset.

Quantitative evidence is heavily dependent on VIEScore (GPT-4.1 based). No evaluation prompts or detailed protocol are provided. The photometric reprojection loss improvement over the strongest baseline is marginal (0.076 vs 0.077/0.082), so the consistency gain is less convincing than the large VIEScore gap suggests.

Technical details are insufficient for reproducibility: the anchor reward's λ is unspecified, reward normalization and VGGT input resolution are unclear, and Eq. (1) in Sec. 3.3 contains an obvious typo ('geo - geo'). These omissions make it difficult to assess or reproduce the training objective.

The method depends on GT camera poses for both relative-pose rewards and final 3DGS reconstruction. This is standard for some 3D editing settings, but it limits the method's applicability and should be explicitly discussed as a constraint.

The ablation study is narrow: all ablations are on face scenes, so conclusions about reward design, anchor strategy, and denoising steps may not transfer to broader scene types. Training cost is also high (42 hours on one GPU for a very small dataset), raising questions about scalability.

strengths: Presents a genuinely novel and timely idea: using reinforcement learning with a 3D foundation model as a verifier to bypass the scarcity of paired multi-view 3D-consistent editing data.

The reward design is well motivated and thoughtfully constructed: VGGT confidence maps, relative pose reward, and anchor-based quality reward are complementary and supported by empirical analysis and ablations.

The paper convincingly demonstrates that VGGT is a more robust verifier than traditional consistency measures, with informative ablation results showing SfM and photometric reprojection rewards are easily reward-hacked.
Strong quantitative results are reported across several metrics (VIEScore, CLIP-dir, Ph-Loss, editing time), with large gains in editing fidelity and a practical inference speedup.

Qualitative results cover diverse and challenging edit types, including motion, replacement, style, background change, and scene addition, and the method generalizes to unseen instructions and scenes in the zero-shot setting.
The framework is flexible and does not require per-scene fine-tuning at inference; the extension to Qwen-Image-Edit suggests applicability beyond a single 2D editor.
The paper is generally clear, includes limitations, and promises code/model release, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The training scale is very limited: 8 scenes, 70 prompts, and about 1.3K samples. Most evaluation cases are novel views of training scenes/instructions, so broad 3D editing generalization is not fully established. Zero-shot evaluation covers only 4 new scenes and 16 unseen instructions, which is relatively small.

The comparison protocol is not fully symmetric. Baselines perform per-scene optimization on test scenes/instructions, while the proposed method is trained on a small set of scenes and then evaluated both in-distribution and zero-shot. This makes it difficult to isolate the contribution of RL 3D consistency learning from other factors, even though the zero-shot results are promising.

VGGT confidence is used as a proxy for 3D consistency based on a controlled replacement experiment. This evidence is useful but does not fully rule out failure modes where VGGT confidently predicts plausible-but-wrong geometry or where certain edit types systematically confuse the reward model.

The anchor reward depends on offline single-view FLUX-Kontext edits. The quality filtering is only heuristically described, and it is unclear how anchor errors or biases affect the RL optimization in harder cases.

Main ablation studies are conducted only on face scenes with roughly 200 samples. The authors argue this is sufficient, but the evidence for scaling these conclusions to full 3D scene editing is limited.

Several metrics lack statistical reporting or confidence intervals. The Ph-Loss improvement in the main comparison is marginal (0.076 vs. 0.077 for GaussCtrl), and its reliability for geometry-changing edits is not fully analyzed.
There are minor technical presentation issues, e.g., the VGGT geometric loss equation in Section 3.3 appears to have a typo or missing target term, which should be corrected.

Some references in the supplementary/method sections appear tangential to the core contribution (e.g., citations on unrelated segmentation, point cloud completion, diffusion acceleration, and 4D perception). These should be removed or explicitly justified to avoid the appearance of citation padding.
